definitions.definition: 'Lord'; the title of the perfected masters of the tradition (Ādinātha, Matsyendranātha, Gorakṣanātha) and the name-ending taken by initiated yogīs; in the Kaulajñānanirṇaya the jīva itself is called the lord (nātha), the all-pervading Śiva.
A perfected one — master of yoga who has conquered time and roams the cosmos (HYP 1.9); the Nāths count nine Nāths and eighty-four siddhas.

cross_language.note: the Tamil Siddhars; overlapping but distinct lineage

definitions.definition: A Nāth ascetic; in north India also the name of householder communities of Nāth descent who sing the Nāth sagas.
'Split-ear': a Nāth yogī whose ear cartilages have been split at initiation to wear the large earrings; such an initiate is also called darśanī.
A Nāth initiate who has received the first initiation (mantra, top-knot cut, black thread) but not yet the ear-splitting.
A name for Aghora ascetics; in Aghora usage the one who has passed beyond all distinctions.
A fully initiated Nāth yogī wearing the earrings called darśan.
The large earrings (of horn, glass or other material) worn in the split ear-cartilage — the chief mark of the Nāth yogī; also called kuṇḍal.
The small horn whistle, worn on the black woollen thread (selī), blown by Nāth yogīs before meals and worship; an outward sign of the inner unstruck sound.
The black woollen cord worn by Nāth yogīs, carrying the nād horn; it takes the place of the brahmin's sacred thread.
The sacred fire kept burning at a Nāth seat or by a wandering yogī; at Gorakhpur an 'unbroken' dhūnī is ascribed to Gorakhnāth; its ash is given as blessing.
The fire of the Aghora ascetic, often kept in or near the cremation ground.
The Nāth greeting and response ('ādeś, ādeś'), acknowledging the command/presence of the Lord in the other.
The 'unmarked, invisible' — a Nāth name for the supreme, called out in the begging cry 'alakh!' and joined with nirañjan ('alakh nirañjan').

equivalents.note: joined as one epithet in the Nāth cry 'alakh nirañjan'

definitions.definition: 'Spotless': the supreme free of all stain and states, abiding subtly within the mind (AmŚ 39–40); one of the synonyms of the highest state (HYP 4.4).
The spotless one beyond the centres, known by piercing them (Yogaviṣaya 10).

cross_language.note: in Bengal also a name of the deity Dharma

definitions.definition: The yogī who has 'shaken off' all conventions and bonds and abides in the supreme state; the ideal described in the sixth upadeśa of the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati; addressed in Hindi as 'avadhū'.
A sub-order of the Nāth yogīs; tradition counts twelve (bārah panth).
The twelve sub-orders of the Nāth yogīs, said to have been set in order by Gorakhnāth (six from Śiva's and six from Gorakh's panths in one telling).
The yogī's garb and, by extension, the Nāth order as a body ('the bhekh of the twelve panths').
Head of a Nāth monastery (maṭh), e.g. the mahant of the Gorakhnāth Maṭh at Gorakhpur.
The begging bowl of the yogī.
The skull or skull-shaped bowl from which the Aghora ascetic eats and drinks.
The patched cloak of the wandering yogī, a mark of the Nāth guise in poetry (e.g. Padmāvat).
Sacred ash from the dhūnī, smeared on the body and given as blessing; in the common legend Gorakh is born from Matsyendra's ash.
Ash of the cremation ground smeared on the body.
'Gorakh's puzzle': a ring-and-wire puzzle associated with Nāth yogīs and, by extension, any intractable entanglement — an image of the world's tangle that only the yogī's knowledge unties.

notes: Popular usage; meaning in the tradition recalled in outline.

definitions.definition: A Nāth monastery (Gorakhpur, Tilla Jogian, Kadri, Dhinodhar, Asthal Bohar and others).
The true guru, by whose grace alone the body and the supreme state come to one taste (SSP 5); the 'guru-ful' drink the nectar, the guru-less go thirsty.
One without a guru, who 'goes away thirsty' from the nectar-well (Gorakh Bānī); its opposite is sagurā.
A short aphoristic saying (from śabda, 'word') of Gorakh or another Nāth, the main form of the Gorakh Bānī.
Vernacular mantras, often ending in an oath by Gorakh or the Nāths, credited with power without the rules of Sanskrit mantras; the tradition ascribes them to Gorakhnāth.
The body as the microcosm of the whole cosmos; the SSP's six upadeśas are organised around the piṇḍa (its origin, knowledge, vision, support and samarasa with the pada).
The 'place' among the four (piṇḍa, pada, rūpa, rūpātīta) of the Kula aim (KJN 3.4).

notes: Homonym of piṇḍa, the rice-ball offered to ancestors (other units' definitions).

definitions.definition: The supreme state ('the state') with which the body is brought to one taste (piṇḍa-pada-samarasa); 'param pad' in Hindi.
Meditation, the second of the four (KJN 3.4).
The cosmic egg — the universe, all of which is found within the body (piṇḍa).
Awareness of the body as containing the cosmos (SSP 3).
The supreme body — the first of the bodies emanated from the Supreme before the human body (SSP 1).
The Supreme's own power, the first to come forth in the origin of the body (SSP 1).
The nine centres of the body taught in the SSP (2).
The sixteen supports (places of fixation) of the body, to be known by the yogī (GŚ-Briggs 13; SSP 2).
The three aims (inner, outer, middle) of the yogī's attention (GŚ-Briggs 13; SSP 2).
The five voids or spaces to be known in the body (GŚ-Briggs 13; SSP 2).
A centre (wheel/lotus) of the body; Nāth texts count six (Yogaviṣaya, GŚ), nine (SSP) or eleven (KJN).
The yoni-place between the root and svādhiṣṭhāna centres, called Kāmarūpa/Kāmākhyā (GŚ 10–11).
The land (Assam) where the Kaula scripture is 'in every house of the yoginīs' and the seat Kāmākhyā (KJN 8.20; 22.10–12).
A sacred seat of the Goddess and yoginīs: Kāmākhyā, Pūrṇagiri, Oḍiyāna, Arbuda with their sub-seats (KJN 8.20–22).
The channel on the left, of the moon (GŚ 20, 23).
The channel on the right, of the sun (GŚ 20, 23).
The central channel of fire, through which awakened kuṇḍalinī rises (GŚ 31); the 'middle path' the breath must enter (HYP 4.114).
The moon at the root of the palate, made of nectar, raining downward (GŚ 57–58); the left side and left nostril (AmŚ 71).
The sun at the navel, of burning nature, that devours the moon's nectar (GŚ 57–58); the right side (AmŚ 71).
The nectar of immortality flowing from the moon at the head; retaining it the body does not decay (GŚ 57–66).
The nectar without which there is no immortality; 'the Kaula nature, of the nature of kāmakalā' (KJN 14.94).
The vital drop (semen/seed) whose retention is life and whose fall is death (HYP 3.88); arising from the mind as ghee from milk (Candrāvalokana).
One whose seed flows upward — a sign of the nectar-filled yogī's body (GŚ 65; KJN 14.57).

The tenth door of the body: in the Amaraughaśāsana the opening of the śaṅkhinī between the royal teeth through which nectar flows, twofold as the path of nectar and the path of death (AmŚ 32, 70); in Hindi Nāth and Sant usage the opening at the crown.

equivalents.note: Hindi usage places the tenth door at the crown; the Amaraughaśāsana locates it at the śaṅkhinī-mouth in the palate

definitions.definition: The aperture of Brahman at the crown; place of the space-concentration that opens the door of liberation (GŚ 73) and through which the jīva departs when the skull splits (KJN 20.2).
'The end of the twelve' above the head, where the haṃsa dissolves and a throbbing garland of jewels is seen (KJN 13.6; 17.18).
The 'circle of the sky' in the head, where the upside-down well of nectar is (Gorakh Bānī).
The 'triple peak' between the brows where the three channels meet (Hindi Nāth and Sant usage).
The 'bee's cave' in the head, a place of inner absorption in Hindi Nāth and Sant songs.
The coiled power lying eightfold above the bulb, closing the door of Brahman, awakened by the fire of yoga or by the guru's grace to rise through suṣumṇā (GŚ 30–31; HYP 3.2).
One of the names of Śiva's Will-power (KJN 20.11); in the Akulavīra the kuṇḍalī is the 'made' (kṛtaka) path, the innate abiding in samarasa (B.43).
The world-mother, pedestal of the liṅga of the void (Jñāneśvarī 6.272–273), coiled three and a half times (6.223).
Śiva's power, inseparable from him (KJN 17.8); as Will she is Vyomamālinī, Khecarī, Kuṇḍalī, Manonmanī (20.10–11); also the female partner of Kaula rites.
The power supporting the body (piṇḍādhāra) (SSP 4).
The jīva as the breath-syllable 'haṃsa', the 'person' of Śakti, moving up and down and dissolving at the dvādaśānta (KJN 6.5; 13.2; 17.18).
The word dwelling in the bodies of breathing beings, repeated naturally 21,600 times a day and called 'so 'ham' (Yogaviṣaya 28–29).
'I am He': the haṃsa heard in reverse, the natural mantra of the breath (Yogaviṣaya 29).
The 'unrepeated' repetition — the haṃsa mantra made by the breath itself (Yogaviṣaya 28–29; KJN 13.2).
The unstruck inner sound heard in the heart and the sky of the head; the 'bull bound threefold roars' at anāhata (GŚ 60); in Hindi 'anahad nād'.
Inner sound, manifesting when the channels are purified (GŚ-Briggs 101); with bindu and Śakti one of three objects of meditation (KJN 5.31).
The seal of the tongue turned back into the cavity of the skull with the gaze between the brows (GŚ 34); a restricted practice.
Also a name of Śakti, 'moving in the sky' (KJN 20.10), and of the class of sky-going yoginīs.
A seal for drawing up and preserving bindu, in the context of which the HYP states that death comes by the fall of bindu (HYP 3.83–89); restricted, summary only.
A variant of vajrolī named in the haṭha texts associated with the Nāths; restricted, not described.
A variant of vajrolī named in the haṭha texts; restricted, not described.
A lock: uḍḍiyāna, jālandhara and mūla are among the five seals whose knower is fit for success (GŚ 32–37).
The abdominal lock between genitals and navel, 'the lion to the elephant of death' (GŚ 35).
The throat lock, by which the nectar does not fall into the fire (GŚ 36).
The root lock drawing apāna upward (GŚ 37).
In the haṭha sense, the 'great seal', a posture-and-breath practice destroying sins (GŚ 32–33).

notes: Homonym of the Buddhist Mahāmudrā (U46); only the haṭha sense is defined here.

definitions.definition: The 'reversed practice' — navel above, palate below, sun above, moon below — by which the nectar is saved from the sun; obtained from the guru's mouth (GŚ 59).
'Force': the yoga of the body and breath taught by Ādinātha as a stairway to rājayoga (HYP 1.1); later texts gloss ha and ṭha as sun and moon.
The royal yoga, the goal to which haṭha leads; synonymous with samādhi, unmanī, sahaja and the rest (HYP 4.3–4).
Dissolution of mind and breath into the supreme; one of the four yogas and a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.3).
The mind-less state beyond mind, in which one is not roused even by drums (KJN 14.83–85); a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.3).
The mind 'beyond mind' by which one is liberated here (KJN 13.5); the fourth mind beyond the guṇas (Jñānakārikā 2.8).
Synonym of unmanī and samādhi (HYP 4.3); also a name of Śakti (KJN 20.11).
The innate, natural state: sahaja-samādhi, in which the mind sees the mind, is liberation (AmŚ 54); sahajā is a synonym of rājayoga and samādhi (HYP 4.4).
The innate principle abiding in the heart (KJN 17.5, 17.21); the innate Kaula path abiding in samarasa, as against the 'made' (kṛtaka) path of kuṇḍalī (Akulavīra B.43).

equivalents.note: HYP lists sahajā among the names of the one highest state

definitions.definition: The void: the breath's path through the void becomes the royal road (HYP 3.3); the mind made 'void of void' in unmanī (KJN 14.84); in Hindi Nāth sayings 'sunn', the place of the supreme.
Equal taste, one-flavouredness: samādhi is the samarasa oneness when breath is exhausted and mind dissolved (GŚ 94); the samarasa of body and supreme state (SSP 5).
The state in which the Akulavīra is seen everywhere and 'all is samarasa' (Akulavīra A.24, A.41).
Absorption: the samarasa of breath and mind (GŚ 94); also, among Nāths, the tomb in which a yogī's body is buried seated.
Liberation while living: the state in which the mind is the seed and the spotless (AmŚ 57–59); a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4).
Perfection of the body: the deathless, adamantine body of the siddha, gained by retaining bindu and nectar.
The perfected body of the Nāth siddha — deathless, unageing, not cut by weapons — as distinct from the Gauḍīya inner devotional body of the same name.
The divine body of the perfected yogī (a Nāth synonym of siddha-deha).
'Making adamantine': the practice in the bone-circle by which 'a man becomes like a thunderbolt' and the body has no dissolution (KJN 15, 'paramavajrīkaraṇa').
Deathlessness: a synonym of the highest state (HYP 4.3); in the Kaula texts attained by devotion to guru and yoginīs and by the nectar meditations (KJN 5.33).
Unageing and deathless — the Nāth ideal of the perfected yogī (GŚ 56 'ajarāmara').
'Cheating time (death)': the yoga that overcomes death (GŚ 2; HYP 3.3).
Taught by Bhairava as the most secret practice; placing the mind in the heart until unmanī destroys death (KJN 6.16–28).
The conquest of death by the nectar meditations (KJN 5).
Reversed practice: turning the downward flows (breath, bindu, nectar, mind) upward — the viparīta-karaṇa of the Sanskrit texts (GŚ 59).
Upside-down speech: paradoxical riddles (the well upside down in the sky, the woman enjoyed by two) used by the Nāths and after them by Kabīr to point to reversed practice.
'Twilight' (intentional) language of the siddhas, shared by Nāth and Buddhist siddha songs; the Nāth vernacular form is the ulaṭbāṃsī.
Restraint and moderation — the Nāth middle way ('one crosses over by restraint alone', Gorakh Bānī).

notes: Distinct from the technical Pātañjala saṃyama (dhāraṇā-dhyāna-samādhi together).

definitions.definition: The 'banana-grove' kingdom of women in which Matsyendra forgot himself until awakened by Gorakṣa; a Nāth image of forgetfulness through sense-life.
The Kaula of the yoginīs, the name the Kaulajñānanirṇaya gives itself in its colophons, brought down by Macchaghnapāda from Candradvīpa.
The 'family' — the domain of Śakti in the body and cosmos; the Kula aim, foundation and scripture (KJN 2.10; 3.1).
What is beyond the Kula, Śiva's own abode, where Bhairava abides at the end of aeons (KJN 16.41); the nectar is 'beyond Akula and Kula' (14.97).
'The hero beyond the Kula': the single reality beyond all distinctions, the same in all, in which all dharmas dissolve (Akulavīra A.3–41).

equivalents.note: the Akulavīra is the Akula as realised 'hero'; the text does not itself equate the words

definitions.definition: The liṅga abiding in the body, worshipped mentally with eight inner flowers, in place of liṅgas of stone, wood or clay (KJN 3.24–31).
The meeting with the yoginīs — a sign and power of Kaula practice (KJN 7.22; 16.8).
The Kaula sacrificial food (caru) of the non-dual rite (caru-advaita), including substances ordinarily forbidden; restricted, summary only (KJN 11).
The bound 'animal' — one whose tendency is outward, who worships external liṅgas or falls from the pledge (KJN 3.17, 3.31, 11.4).
One bound by the eight fetters (Kulārṇava 13.91).
The 'hero' — the qualified Kaula adept, truthful, free of anger, knowing the Śakti born of the body and formed by non-dual conduct (KJN 20.18–22).
'Made' — the Kaula path of effort in which kuṇḍalī is impelled by seals and mantras, contrasted with the innate (sahaja) (Akulavīra B.43–45).
'Not terrible' (a-ghora): the benign-terrible face of Śiva, name of one of the five Brahma-mantras; the lineage takes it as its name, holding that nothing is to be feared or shunned as impure.

notes: The Aghora Brahma-mantra is in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka's tenth book (chapter-level ref; not checked).

definitions.definition: An ascetic of the Aghora lineage.
Non-discrimination, non-difference: seeing no division of pure and impure, high and low, since Śiva is in all.
The non-dual conduct (advaitācāra) of the Kaula (KJN 11.3–4).
The eight fetters — disgust, doubt, fear, shame, loathing, family, conduct, caste; one bound by them is a paśu, one freed is Maheśvara (Kulārṇava 13.90–91).
Disgust — first of the eight fetters, overcome in Aghora practice.
The cremation ground, the Aghora ascetic's place of practice and dwelling.
The skull, 'best of all vessels' for the Kaula rite (KJN 12.13).
The skull bowl carried by the Aghora ascetic.
Practice seated on a corpse in the cremation ground, attributed to Aghora and Śākta adepts; restricted — summary only.
The Goddess of the Hiṅglāj seat in Balochistan, venerated in Aghora as the lineage goddess; Kīnārām is said to have gone there.
The tank at Kīnārām Sthal, Śivālā, Varanasi — the chief seat of the Aghora lineage, whose water is held to heal.
'Lady of all': the Goddess after whom the Śrī Sarveśvarī Samūh of Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām is named.
